questions.question: According to the Central Limit Theorem, what becomes approximately normal as the sample size grows?
options: The distribution of the sample mean
questions.explanation: The CLT is about the sampling distribution of the mean (and sums). The raw data and the population keep whatever shape they had.

questions.question: A common rule of thumb for the CLT to work well is...
questions.explanation: n ≥ 30 is the usual guideline. Strongly skewed populations may need more, and bell-shaped ones need far fewer.

questions.question: A population has μ = 80 and σ = 20. For n = 100, the sample mean is approximately normal with what mean and SD?
Using the same population (μ = 80, σ = 20) and n = 100, what is P(x̄ > 83)?
A bag process has μ = 300 g and σ = 12 g. A sample of 36 bags has a mean of 296 g. What is P(x̄ < 296) if the process is on target?
questions.explanation: SE = 12/6 = 2, so z = (296 − 300)/2 = −2, and P(Z < −2) = 0.0228. A small probability suggests the process may be underfilling.

questions.question: Which statement about n ≥ 30 is correct?
options: It makes the data normally distributed
It makes the sample mean approximately normal, while the data can remain skewed
It removes the need for random sampling
questions.explanation: Large n smooths out the distribution of the mean. It does nothing for the shape of the data and cannot repair a biased or non-random sample.
